title: Cat Scratch, Barnyard Air and the Select Agent List
summary: Learn the typical course and management of cat scratch disease, how Coxiella burnetii reaches people (and why ticks are not the main route), the 2007–2010 Dutch Q fever epidemic, and which rickettsial agents are on the US select agent list.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 63 Hit 10 (cat scratch disease), Hit 11 (select agent status) and Hit 12 (Q fever transmission and the Netherlands outbreak). Checked against Nawrocki 2020, Nelson 2016, Mazur-Melewska 2015, Tan 2024, Celina 2022, de Koeijer 2020, Wielders 2014, Panning 2008, 42 CFR 73.3 (eCFR version 2026-10-01) and the 2012 final rule (77 FR 61084, read as GPO text on govinfo.gov; federalregister.gov returned an access-request page). The reviewer’s “category B” for C. burnetii is true but incomplete: C. burnetii is also a listed HHS select agent (register flag rv-coxiella-select-agent-too). “Not by tick bite” is qualified: tick bites are a reported but non-essential route (rv-q-fever-tick-route). “No antibiotics needed” for typical CSD is qualified: azithromycin can be considered for significant lymphadenopathy (rv-csd-azithromycin-option). Not taught: disseminated CSD regimens, the Number Vault, the chapter figure. The CDC Q fever MMWR (Anderson 2013) returned 403 and Eldin 2017 had no open full text; neither was used.

objectives: Describe the typical course of cat scratch disease and when antibiotics are considered.
State the main route of human Coxiella burnetii infection and the role of ticks.
Identify which rickettsial agents are on the US HHS select agent list and which was removed in 2012.

scenes.title: A kitten, a goat farm and a freezer
scenes.altText: Invented scenario: three problems reach the microbiology bench. (1) A healthy teenager has a small papule at a kitten scratch and a tender axillary lymph node for two weeks. (2) A man living near a dairy goat farm has fever and pneumonia; a colleague asks which tick bit him. (3) A US freezer inventory lists isolates of Rickettsia prowazekii, Coxiella burnetii and Rickettsia rickettsii. Question token: “Treat, trace, or register?”

cues.text: Three problems reach the bench. A healthy teenager has a small bump at a kitten scratch and a tender lymph node in the armpit.
A man living near a dairy goat farm has fever and pneumonia, and a colleague asks which tick bit him.
And a freezer inventory in a US lab lists three organisms. Which need treatment, which need tracing, and which need registering?

scenes.title: Cat scratch disease
scenes.altText: Schematic: cat, cat flea and a human hand. Bartonella henselae is maintained and spread among cats by the cat flea (Ctenocephalides felis); humans are infected through cat scratches and possibly bites. Typical course card: papule at the inoculation site 3–10 days after inoculation, then regional lymphadenopathy 1–3 weeks after inoculation, in the nodes draining the site. 80–95% of cases are typical; 5–20% are atypical (eye, nervous system, liver/spleen, heart, bone). Management card: most cases are self-limited and need no antibiotics; for significant lymphadenopathy azithromycin can be considered and has been shown to speed recovery.

cues.text: Cat scratch disease is caused by Bartonella henselae. Cat fleas spread it among cats, and people catch it through a scratch, and possibly a bite.
The typical picture: a papule at the scratch site three to ten days later, then a swollen regional lymph node one to three weeks after the scratch, in the nodes that drain that site.
Eighty to ninety-five percent of cases look like this. Five to twenty percent are atypical, involving the eye, nervous system, liver and spleen, heart or bone.
Most typical cases are self-limited and need no antibiotics. For a large, troublesome node, azithromycin can be considered, and it has been shown to speed recovery.

props.title: Bartonella henselae
lines: Cat flea spreads it among cats

scenes.title: Q fever travels on the air
scenes.altText: Schematic: a goat herd at kidding season and a plume of dust drifting toward houses. Source card: domestic ruminants (cattle, sheep, goats) are the most frequent sources of human infection; infected females shed very large numbers of Coxiella burnetii in birth products at parturition, and also in urine, faeces and milk. Route card: inhalation of contaminated dust and aerosols is the main route of human infection. Tick card: ticks can carry C. burnetii and tick bites are a reported route, but ticks are not essential for transmission. Outbreak card: the Netherlands 2007–2010 epidemic, linked to infected dairy goat farms, produced over 4000 notified human cases, the largest recorded Q fever epidemic.

cues.text: Coxiella burnetii, the Q fever agent, lives mainly in cattle, sheep and goats. Infected females shed huge numbers of bacteria in birth products when they give birth, and also in urine, faeces and milk.
People catch it mainly by breathing contaminated dust and aerosols, by close contact with animals, or from air blowing off a farm.
Ticks can carry the organism, and tick bites are a reported route, but unlike most vector-borne infections, ticks are not needed for transmission.
The largest recorded epidemic hit the Netherlands from 2007 to 2010. Infected dairy goat farms were the source, and over four thousand human cases were notified.

props.label: Main route: inhaled dust and aerosols

scenes.title: Which agents are on the select agent list?
scenes.altText: US select agent card (42 CFR 73.3, HHS list): Coxiella burnetii and Rickettsia prowazekii are listed HHS select agents; neither is marked Tier 1. 2012 biennial review card (77 FR 61084): R. rickettsii was removed (poor environmental stability, no person-to-person spread without a vector, effective antibiotics, hard to grow in quantity); R. prowazekii was retained (studied as a weapon by offensive programmes, infectious dose estimated as low as 10 organisms, no licensed US vaccine); C. burnetii was retained (environmental stability, ease of transmission, extremely low infectious dose, history of weaponisation). C. burnetii is also a CDC category B bioterrorism agent. Hook answers card.

cues.text: In the United States, the HHS select agent list in federal regulation includes both Coxiella burnetii and Rickettsia prowazekii. Neither is a Tier 1 agent.
Rickettsia rickettsii was removed in the 2012 review: it is unstable in the environment, does not spread person to person without a vector, responds to antibiotics and is hard to grow in quantity.

Rickettsia prowazekii stayed: it was studied as a weapon, its infectious dose may be as low as ten organisms, and there is no licensed US vaccine. Coxiella stayed for its stability, very low infectious dose and history of weaponisation. It is also a CDC category B agent.
Back to the hook. The teenager needs reassurance and follow-up. The man most likely breathed farm aerosols. And the two organisms still on the list must be registered.

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards: “Q fever is a tick-borne disease” (✓ mainly inhaled aerosols and dust from infected animals; ticks are not essential); “Rickettsia rickettsii is a select agent” (✓ removed in the 2012 biennial review; R. prowazekii and C. burnetii remain); “Every cat scratch node needs antibiotics” (✓ most typical cases are self-limited; azithromycin is optional for significant lymphadenopathy).

cues.text: Trap one: Q fever is a tick-borne disease. No: people catch it mainly by inhaling aerosols and dust from infected animals; ticks are not essential.
Trap two: Rickettsia rickettsii is a select agent. No: it was removed in 2012. Rickettsia prowazekii and Coxiella burnetii remain.
Trap three: every cat scratch node needs antibiotics. No: most typical cases settle on their own.

props.title: ✗ “Q fever = tick bite.”
lines: ✓ Mainly inhaled aerosols; ticks not essential

scenes.title: Scratch, sniff, lock
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “SCRATCH, SNIFF, LOCK: cat scratch disease starts with a SCRATCH and usually settles on its own; Q fever comes from a SNIFF of barnyard air; and the freezer LOCK is for prowazekii and Coxiella, not rickettsii since 2012.” Tokens: scratch = Bartonella · sniff = Coxiella · lock = select agents. A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: scratch, sniff, lock. Cat scratch disease starts with a scratch and usually settles by itself. Q fever comes from a sniff of barnyard air. And the freezer lock is for prowazekii and Coxiella, not rickettsii since 2012.

Where it breaks: five to twenty percent of cat scratch cases are atypical and may need treatment; ticks and raw milk are rarer Q fever routes; and the select agent list is US law that is reviewed and can change.

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “Cat scratch disease: papule + regional node, usually self-limited · Q fever: inhaled aerosols from infected ruminants, ticks not essential”, “US select agents: Rickettsia prowazekii + Coxiella burnetii · Rickettsia rickettsii removed 2012”.

cues.text: Typical cat scratch disease is a self-limited papule and regional node, Q fever is caught mainly by inhaling aerosols from infected livestock rather than from ticks, and on the US select agent list Rickettsia prowazekii and Coxiella burnetii remain while Rickettsia rickettsii was removed in 2012.

props.label: CSD: papule + node, self-limited · Q fever: inhaled, ticks not essential
Select agents: R. prowazekii + C. burnetii · R. rickettsii removed 2012

explanation.what: Plain language: a kitten scratch can cause a bump and a swollen gland that usually go away on their own; Q fever is mostly caught by breathing air contaminated by infected farm animals, especially around birthing; and US law tightly controls a short list of dangerous microbes, which includes the epidemic typhus agent and the Q fever agent but no longer the Rocky Mountain spotted fever agent. Scientific terms: Bartonella henselae, Ctenocephalides felis, inoculation papule, regional lymphadenopathy, atypical cat scratch disease, Coxiella burnetii, parturition, aerosol, HHS select agent, Tier 1, biennial review, CDC category B.
explanation.why: Cat scratch disease usually resolves because the immunocompetent host contains the infection in the draining nodes. C. burnetii is shed massively in birth products and is environmentally stable, so contaminated dust carries it far from farms. Select agent status reflects bioweapon potential: stability, infectious dose, transmissibility and treatability.
explanation.measure: CSD: papule 3–10 days after inoculation, node 1–3 weeks; 80–95% typical, 5–20% atypical. Q fever: main route inhalation; Netherlands 2007–2010 > 4000 notified cases. Select agents (42 CFR 73.3): C. burnetii and R. prowazekii listed (not Tier 1); R. rickettsii removed 2012 (77 FR 61084).
explanation.differs: Typical vs atypical CSD; inhaled vs tick-borne Q fever; HHS select agent (regulatory list) vs CDC category B (bioterrorism priority category); R. prowazekii (retained) vs R. rickettsii (removed).
explanation.examAngle: Expect: manage a healthy patient with a scratch-site papule and regional node, pick the transmission route for a farmer with Q fever, or choose which rickettsial organism is (or is no longer) a select agent.

questions.stem: A healthy 14-year-old has a small papule at a kitten scratch on the forearm and a tender epitrochlear lymph node for 2 weeks. He is otherwise well. Which statement best fits?

options.text: Typical cat scratch disease, usually self-limited; antibiotics are optional for significant lymphadenopathy
options.rationale: Correct. Most cases are typical and self-limited; azithromycin can be considered for significant lymphadenopathy and speeds recovery.

options.text: Q fever acquired from the kitten’s fleas
options.rationale: Incorrect. Cat fleas spread Bartonella henselae among cats; Q fever is mainly acquired by inhaling aerosols from infected animals.

options.text: Disseminated bartonellosis that always needs prolonged combination therapy
options.rationale: Incorrect. A papule with a regional node in a healthy host is the typical, localised form.

options.text: Rocky Mountain spotted fever needing select agent reporting
options.rationale: Incorrect. The picture is cat scratch disease, and Rickettsia rickettsii is no longer a select agent.

questions.stem: During a large Q fever epidemic, residents near infected dairy goat farms fall ill. What is the main route of human infection?

options.text: Inhalation of dust and aerosols contaminated by infected animals
options.rationale: Correct. Inhalation is the main route; birth products shed very large numbers of organisms.

options.text: Bites of ticks, which are essential vectors
options.rationale: Incorrect. Tick bites are a reported route, but ticks are not essential for transmission.
Incorrect. The sources are infected animals and their contaminated environment.

options.text: Bites of the human body louse
options.rationale: Incorrect. Human infection comes mainly from inhaling material from infected animals, chiefly ruminants; lice are not the described route.

questions.stem: Which organism was removed from the US HHS select agent list in the 2012 biennial review?

options.rationale: Correct. It was removed for poor environmental stability, no person-to-person spread without a vector, effective antibiotics and difficulty of culture.
Incorrect. It was retained (weapons history, very low estimated infectious dose, no licensed US vaccine).
Incorrect. It was retained and is still listed in 42 CFR 73.3; it is also a CDC category B agent.
Incorrect. It remains listed as a Tier 1 select agent.

accuracyFlags.issue: Ch. 63 Hit 11 contrasts R. prowazekii as a select agent with C. burnetii as “category B”. 42 CFR 73.3 lists C. burnetii as an HHS select agent as well, and the 2012 final rule explicitly retained it; category B is a separate CDC bioterrorism category (register flag rv-coxiella-select-agent-too).

Ch. 63 Hit 12 says C. burnetii spreads “not by tick bite”. Inhalation is the main route, but Celina 2022 lists tick bites as a reported route while noting ticks are not essential; the lesson teaches ticks as a non-essential route (register flag rv-q-fever-tick-route).

Ch. 63 Hit 10 says typical cat scratch disease needs no antibiotics. Mazur-Melewska 2015 agrees most cases are self-limited but notes azithromycin speeds recovery and can be considered for significant lymphadenopathy; the source gives 80–95% typical (Nawrocki 2020) (register flag rv-csd-azithromycin-option).
The select agent list is US federal regulation (42 CFR 73). Philippine biosafety and biosecurity rules are not covered; MTLE candidates should check local requirements.
